ch11.d.sys: A puck on a string through a hole, or a person on a spinning chair holding dumbbells
ch11.d.mode: Pull the string down through the hole to shorten the radius, or let it out to lengthen it
ch11.d.rIn: Radius with the string pulled in; the outer radius is 1 m
ch11.d.wOut: Angular velocity on the 1 m circle; sets the angular momentum $L$
ch11.d.areas: Sectors swept by the string in equal time intervals $\Delta t$, each with its area measured from the drawn shape; all are equal
ch11.c.d.mode: Pull the arms holding the dumbbells in towards the body, or stretch them out
ch11.c.d.m: Mass $m$ of the dumbbell in each hand
ch11.c.d.wOut: Angular velocity with the arms out (dumbbells at 0.8 m); sets the angular momentum $L$
ch11.s.goal.L: With zero external torque about the axis (the hole), the angular momentum $L = I\omega$ is conserved
ch11.s.goal.I: Mass moved towards the axis lowers the rotational inertia $I$, so the angular velocity rises. Puck: $I = mr^2$; chair: $I = I_0 + 2mr^2$
ch11.s.goal.K: Angular momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not: the force pulling the string, or the arm muscles, do work
ch11.s.obs.flat: $L(t)$ stays flat while the radius changes; $I(t)$ and $\omega(t)$ change in opposite directions
ch11.s.obs.square: Puck: half the radius gives a quarter of $I$ and four times $\omega$ ($\omega \propto 1/r^2$)
ch11.s.obs.ratio: Chair: $\omega_\text{in}/\omega_\text{out} = I_\text{out}/I_\text{in}$, about 2.4 with the defaults (less than 4 because of $I_0$)
ch11.s.obs.work: $K = L^2/2I$ rises when the radius shrinks and falls when it grows; the rise equals the work done by the pulling force or the arm muscles
ch11.s.obs.area: Puck, swept areas: sectors swept in equal times $\Delta t$ (top left) have equal areas, whether long and thin or short and wide; each sector shows its area (the same principle as Kepler's second law, Ch 13)
ch11.s.obs.mass: Chair: heavier dumbbells change $I$ more, so $\omega$ changes more
ch11.s.assume: Puck: frictionless table, massless string, point-like puck; the string is worked so that the radius changes smoothly over 3 s; seen from above. The tension $T \propto 1/r^3$ changes by up to 37 times, so its arrow is proportional to $T$ above a minimum length
ch11.c.assume: Chair: frictionless axle; body and chair have $I_0 = 1.5$ kg·m²; point-like dumbbells, massless arms; dumbbells at 0.8 m ↔ 0.2 m (over 2 s); seen from above
ch11.r.d.theta: Angle $\theta$ between the incline and the horizontal
ch11.r.d.focus: Body whose contact-point, centre and top velocities are drawn and whose energies are plotted
ch11.r.goal.roll: Rolling without slipping: $v_\text{cm} = \omega R$; the contact point is momentarily at rest and the top moves at $2v_\text{cm}$
ch11.r.goal.race: Acceleration down the incline $a = g\sin\theta/(1+\beta)$ with $\beta = I_\text{cm}/MR^2$: hoop 1, disk 1/2, solid sphere 2/5, so the mass distribution alone fixes the order. Each lane is tagged with its body's $\beta$ and $a$
ch11.r.obs.contact: Contact point $v = 0$, centre $v_\text{cm}$, top $2v_\text{cm}$: the whole body turns momentarily about the contact point
ch11.r.obs.order: Finishing order: block, sphere, disk, hoop, numbered 1–4 at the finish line. The slope of $v(t)$ is $a$; the area under every line is the 1.6 m run
ch11.r.obs.split: $K_\text{rot}/K_\text{trans} = \beta$ stays constant: the hoop splits its energy in half, the sphere puts only 2/7 into rotation, and more translation means faster
ch11.r.obs.mass: Changing the angle keeps the order and the ratios of the accelerations; mass and radius do not matter either
ch11.r.obs.block: The frictionless block does not turn ($\beta = 0$): $a = g\sin\theta$, and its bottom face moves at $v_\text{cm}$ too
ch11.r.assume: Every body has $M = 1$ kg and $R = 0.12$ m; 1.6 m run; all released from rest together. Round bodies roll without slipping on static friction (no rolling resistance; needs $\mu_s \ge \beta\tan\theta/(1+\beta)$, 0.42 for the hoop at 40°). The block slides without friction. Bodies are drawn stopped at the finish line; played at half speed
